title: [10, 9, 1].sort() returns [1, 10, 9]
assumption: Calling .sort() on an array of numbers sorts them numerically.

input.description: Sorting a plain JavaScript array of numbers (scores, counts, prices) without passing a comparator — the single most common sort call in JavaScript.

why: When no comparator is supplied, the ECMAScript spec has Array.prototype.sort() convert each element to a string and compare the strings (undefined values are set aside and placed at the end). It is never numeric unless you pass a comparator. As strings, "10" < "9" is true, because "1" has a lower code unit than "9" and string comparison stops at the first differing character, so 10 sorts before 9. Python's sorted() compares the numbers themselves, so this failure does not exist there.
fix: Always pass an explicit numeric comparator to Array.prototype.sort() when sorting numbers: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b). There is no "numeric mode" flag — the comparator is the only way to opt out of string comparison.

test_cases.note: A numeric sort should return [1, 9, 10]. An implementation that calls arr.sort() with no comparator returns [1, 10, 9].
